blocks.text: Photo Playground has its roots in photocollage animation and Preschool Pop.

A pioneer of this visual style was animation studio Little Airplane Productions, who began creating their own animations once creative director Jennifer Oxley was hired. For the Wonder Pets! television show that aired on Nickelodeon from 2006 to 2010, Oxley created a technique called "photo-puppetry," one totally unique to their studio. It was done by using photos of real animals, editing them to make them cuter, and then using them as digital puppets -- segmenting them and pinning them at the joints, then manipulating them like paper dolls frame-by-frame. They utilized this technique again in their next show, 3rd & Bird.

Similarly, in 2005, the producers of the television show Little Einsteins were searching for a way to seamlessly blend animation and live-action footage. The show's animation essentially worked like a mixed-media collage -- the backgrounds and accessories were live-action, but the main characters were 2D vector animations added on top and drop shades were used to create depth. This helped the creators of the show incorporate real-world art pieces in the program without having to modify or animate them at all.
Other series like Backyardigans used photos of real-life clouds and mountains for backgrounds.
The aesthetic declined in the mid-2010s. One possible reason is advances in rendering took the need out for photobashing outside of specifically wanting it.

The primary link for the aesthetic is the use of photobashing or photopuppetry, CG, and other digital methods to use realistic or semirealistic textures and backgrounds blended with cartoony ones, often resulting in a Liminal Space feel. This can be as simple as just clouds and mountains for the backgrounds. The colour scheme tends towards green, blue, and purple

Common settings include either Arcadian rural valleys, gardens, backyards, parks, or other idyllic greenspaces, or cluttered but homely/pleasant-feeling indoor spaces, like living rooms or bedrooms. Both focus on places and things young children are already familiar with.
Common iconography and subjects include animals (typically domestic or farm animals) and household objects (like toys).
Common themes are play and imagination.
